title: The Courtroom Escape Hatches Sovereign Citizens Swear By

scenes.purpose: Open on the real words a defendant said in court, so the question is concrete from the first second.

visual.description: The trial-court exchange from State v. Smith set as a court record page; the line types into view; "I give the Court no consent" highlights amber as it is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: I give the Court no consent

citations.label: State v. Smith, Ohio Court of Appeals, 2024

scenes.direction: Cold open, no title; slow push on the highlight.
scenes.narration: A man on trial in Ohio told the court he reserved his rights "per UCC 1-308 without prejudice", and then added, "I give the Court no consent".

scenes.purpose: Name the belief behind the words: the right phrase removes the judge's power.

visual.description: Dark field; the words "No power over him" set large in the centre, pushing in slowly.

scenes.direction: Hard cut from the excerpt; the title lands on "no power".
scenes.narration: He believed those words, said in the right place, would leave the judge with no power over him.

scenes.purpose: Pose the video's first question plainly.

visual.description: The question types on word by word in large type; "jurisdiction" turns amber as the last word lands.
onScreenText: Can anything you say, sign or point to take you out of a court's jurisdiction?

scenes.narration: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?

scenes.purpose: Lay out the four parts of the kit the promoters sell, which the investigation then takes one at a time.

visual.description: An open toolkit drawn as four labelled cards that slide out of a case one by one as each is named: 1) a signature line with "UCC 1-308" pencilled beside it, labelled "A code under your signature"; 2) a flag edge with a gold fringe, labelled "A fringe on the flag"; 3) a rolled parchment, labelled "An old act of Congress"; 4) a contract page with a signature line, labelled "Every law is a contract". On s05 each card gains a thin line running down to a ground strip labelled "something real", then a gavel icon appears beside the case. Flat icons only, no people.

scenes.direction: Each card slides out on its noun in s04; the "something real" ground draws in on s05.
scenes.narration: The people who sell this idea offer a whole kit: a code to write under your signature, a fringe on the courtroom flag, an old act of Congress, and the theory that every law is just a contract. Each one leans on something real, so we can look at what it rests on, and then read what courts did when someone tried it.

scenes.purpose: Show the consent claim in a promoter's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "unless you grant them" emphasised as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; quote builds as spoken.
scenes.narration: The kit starts with consent. A channel called Out of Babylon puts it plainly: "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

scenes.purpose: Show the instruction viewers are given for withholding consent.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "UCC 1-308" set in a typewriter face and underlined as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved"

scenes.direction: Quote builds as spoken; hold on the code.
scenes.narration: And the way to withhold that consent, according to The Grown Academy, is to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

scenes.purpose: Read the section itself, so the viewer sees what the code actually says.

visual.description: The text of UCC 1-308(a) as a statute page; the clause about performing with an explicit reservation of rights underlines first, then "without prejudice" highlights amber.

citations.label: Uniform Commercial Code 1-308 and official comment

scenes.direction: Question beat on s08 over the blank page, then the text fades up on s09.
scenes.narration: So what does that code section actually say? It is part of the Uniform Commercial Code, and it says a party that "performs, promises performance, or assents to performance" while explicitly reserving its rights does not lose them; words like "without prejudice" or "under protest" are enough.

scenes.purpose: Show the official comment's stated purpose: keeping a contract going during a dispute.

visual.description: The official comment paragraph beneath the statute text; "despite a pending dispute" highlights as it is spoken.

citations.label: Uniform Commercial Code 1-308 and official comment

scenes.direction: Scroll down from the statute text to the comment.
scenes.narration: The official comment gives its purpose: the continuation of performance "along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

scenes.purpose: Make the commercial purpose concrete with a picture, then rule out courts and criminal law.

visual.description: Flat illustration of a shop counter seen side-on. A delivery truck drops boxes at the door; the shop keeps carrying them in. On the counter an invoice slides in and a red stamp "UNDER PROTEST" lands on it while the boxes keep coming. On s12 the scene shrinks into a card labelled "Commercial contract" on the left; on the right three greyed cards labelled "Courts", "Police" and "Criminal charges" appear and each gets a thin strike-through as it is spoken. No faces; simple icons.

citations.label: Uniform Commercial Code 1-308 and official comment

scenes.direction: Boxes move continuously through s11; the split and strike-throughs time to the nouns in s12. "UNDER PROTEST" is a word from s09; give the stamp its own beat.
scenes.narration: Picture a shop that keeps accepting a supplier's deliveries while it argues about the bill, and doesn't want accepting them to count as dropping the argument. That is the whole job of the section: it is about performing a commercial contract, and it says nothing about courts, police or criminal charges.

scenes.purpose: Return to the man in Ohio and show how the code fared in his own case.

visual.description: The appeals-court opinion page; "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing" highlights amber.

excerpt.highlight: Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing

citations.label: State v. Smith, Ohio Court of Appeals, 2024

scenes.direction: Callback to sc01's page style; hold after the highlight.
scenes.narration: And the man in Ohio? He was found guilty of all four charges, and the appeals court noted that "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

scenes.purpose: Turn from the written code to the spoken claim of no consent.

visual.description: Title card; "out loud" slightly larger than the rest.

scenes.narration: Withholding consent out loud fares no better than writing it down.

scenes.purpose: Show a federal appeals court rejecting the consent claim whatever status is claimed.

visual.description: Benabe opinion text; "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts" highlights on s15, then "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented" underlines on s16.

excerpt.highlight: that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts

scenes.narration: In United States v. Benabe, a federal appeals court wrote that whatever status a person claims, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts". It added that such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

scenes.purpose: Show the same argument failing in another country, and the researchers' plain statement of why.

visual.description: The review's page; "All three were unsuccessful" underlined first, then the closing sentence about consent highlighted amber as it is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it

citations.label: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.narration: Courts in New Zealand heard the same argument from people who said a court's authority depended on their consent, and all three lost; the researchers who reviewed those cases put the problem simply: "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it".

scenes.purpose: Signal the next item in the kit.

visual.description: Title card "The flag" with a thin gold fringe drawn along its lower edge.

scenes.narration: Then there is the flag.

scenes.purpose: Show the flag belief in a believer's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "Admiralty" emphasised.

scenes.narration: A letter in the Mountain Democrat newspaper states the belief in one line: "The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction".

scenes.purpose: Show the court examining the law of the flag and what the Army itself said about fringe.

visual.description: McCann opinion page; "in the interest of killing this argument for good" underlines on s20, then the Adjutant General's line highlights amber on s21.

excerpt.highlight: is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance

scenes.direction: Two marks in order; push in on the second.
scenes.narration: A federal court, noting that other courts had already called the argument frivolous, decided to examine the law of the flag "in the interest of killing this argument for good". It found that the Army's own Adjutant General had written that a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

scenes.purpose: Land the principle that decides the question, in the court's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, large; "law, statute, and constitution" emphasised as spoken.
onScreenText: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game"

scenes.direction: Camera punches on "magic talisman"; hold after.
scenes.narration: Then it said what decides the question: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman".

scenes.purpose: Introduce the corporation claim in a promoter's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "1871" and "corporation" emphasised.
onScreenText: "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation"

scenes.direction: s23 plays over the empty card; quote builds on s24.
scenes.narration: The next trick goes bigger: it says the whole country was quietly turned into a company. The channel SYDLIS says "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

scenes.purpose: Show what the act of 1871 actually did and how briefly that government lasted.

visual.description: A horizontal timeline from 1871 to 1874. At 1871 a marker drops and a box grows labelled "District of Columbia" with the subtitle "a body corporate for municipal purposes"; three icons appear beneath it as spoken: a contract ("make contracts"), a gavel ("sue and be sued"), a street ("its streets"). On s26 the box gains the label "a mere municipal corporation" and an arrow from it points up to a larger box "the government of the United States", tagged "sovereign power". On s27 a marker drops at 1874 and the District box is struck through, labelled "abolished".
onScreenText: a body corporate for municipal purposes
the government of the United States

citations.label: Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia, U.S. Supreme Court, 1889

scenes.direction: Build left to right with the narration; the strike-through lands on "abolished".
scenes.narration: The act of 1871 is real, and the Supreme Court later described what it did: it made the District of Columbia "a body corporate for municipal purposes", a local government that could make contracts, sue and be sued, and look after its streets. The Court called the District "a mere municipal corporation", and said the sovereign power over it was lodged "in the government of the United States". And the government that the 1871 act set up did not even last: an act of 1874 abolished it.

scenes.purpose: Show the broadest claim: every law is only corporate bylaws.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "bylaws" emphasised.
onScreenText: "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation"

scenes.direction: s28 over the empty card; quote builds on s29.
scenes.narration: The last item in the kit is the broadest. Americans In Action says that "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation", rules that, it says, do not bind state nationals.

scenes.purpose: Show a federal appeals court answering the contract theory of tax.

visual.description: Bey v. Indiana opinion text; "We have repeatedly rejected such claims" highlights amber.

excerpt.highlight: We have repeatedly rejected such claims

scenes.narration: In Bey v. Indiana, a man argued that Indiana could not tax him without a contract between them, and the federal appeals court answered: "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".

scenes.purpose: Show the no-consent claim failing on the road in New Zealand, and the reason.

visual.description: The review's page on James v The Corporation New Zealand Police; "abuse of process" underlines on s31, then the sentence about vehicles on public roads highlights on s32.

excerpt.highlight: Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles

citations.label: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.narration: In New Zealand, a self-described freeman said he had never consented to the Land Transport Act and so was not bound by it; the court struck out his claim as an abuse of process. The reason is simple: "Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles".

scenes.purpose: Deliver the first answer: no, in three countries.

visual.description: A large "No" above three country names that build as each is spoken.

citations.label: Netolitzky and Warman, pseudolaw at the Supreme Court of Canada
Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.direction: Each name lands on its word; hold after the last.
scenes.narration: So the answer to the first question is no: courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the idea that their power depends on your consent.

scenes.purpose: Show the Canadian researchers' verdict.

visual.description: The paper's page; "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit" highlights amber.

excerpt.highlight: These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit

citations.label: Netolitzky and Warman, pseudolaw at the Supreme Court of Canada

scenes.narration: Researchers who followed these arguments to the Supreme Court of Canada found that it has never granted one of them leave to appeal, and their verdict is blunt: "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

scenes.purpose: Show the same conclusion from the Australia and New Zealand review.

visual.description: The review's page; "No courts accept these arguments" highlights, then the rest of the sentence underlines.

citations.label: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.narration: A review of cases in Australia and New Zealand reached the same place: "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

scenes.purpose: Be honest that the US evidence is a run of rulings, not a count, then turn to the second question.

visual.description: The Ohio opinion page; "continue to make their way to court and fail" highlights; on s37 the page slides away to a blank field.

excerpt.highlight: continue to make their way to court and fail

citations.label: State v. Smith, Ohio Court of Appeals, 2024

scenes.narration: For the United States, the evidence here has no count like that; what it has is a run of rulings, and the Ohio appeals court summed them up by saying the claims "continue to make their way to court and fail". If nothing you say, sign or point to removes a court's power, the promoters' next offer is to change who you are.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the second question, changing who you are, in a promoter's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "we are not part of that" emphasised.
onScreenText: "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that"

scenes.narration: A channel called Sovereign National describes ordinary citizenship as the thing "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that".

scenes.purpose: Show the roadside promise made for the paperwork.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "has to let you go" emphasised.
onScreenText: "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go"

scenes.narration: Some sellers promise that the paperwork works at the roadside too: SPC University tells viewers that "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go".

scenes.purpose: Read what the law says a national is.

visual.description: The statute definition page; "a citizen of the United States" highlights on s41, then the permanent-allegiance clause underlines.

excerpt.highlight: a citizen of the United States

scenes.direction: Question beat on s40 over the blank page.
scenes.narration: So what is a national, in the law itself? Federal statute defines a national of the United States as "a citizen of the United States", or a person who is not a citizen but owes the country permanent allegiance.

scenes.purpose: Show that every citizen is already a national, and where the other kind comes from.

visual.description: Two nested shapes. An outer circle labelled "national"; inside it a large circle labelled "citizen" fills most of it. The thin crescent of the outer circle left over is labelled "non-citizen" with a small island icon and the words "born in an outlying possession". On "not from a form you file" a paper form icon slides toward the circles and bounces off the outer edge.
onScreenText: not from a form you file

scenes.direction: Circles draw on "every citizen is already a national"; the form bounces on its phrase.
scenes.narration: So every citizen is already a national, and the non-citizen kind comes from the circumstances of birth, such as being born in an outlying possession of the United States, not from a form you file.

scenes.purpose: Show federal appeals courts rejecting state-citizen status in tax cases.

visual.description: The IRS compilation page listing the circuit rulings; "barely worth a footnote" highlights amber.

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments

scenes.narration: Federal appeals courts, in tax cases, have also rejected the related claim that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States puts a person beyond the federal courts; one called it "barely worth a footnote".

scenes.purpose: Explain the Moorish version through a researcher's description of it.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "exempt from normal laws" emphasised.
onScreenText: "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws"

scenes.narration: The Moorish version leans on old treaties instead, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue explains how: "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws".

scenes.purpose: Show the scale of what the Moorish claim was used to demand.

visual.description: One large stat tile: "$11.5 billion", labelled "Refund sought from the State of Indiana".

chart.title: Bey v. Indiana

points.label: Refund sought from the State of Indiana

chart.note: The amount the plaintiff asked for, not anything awarded; the suit was dismissed.

scenes.direction: The figure counts up on "$11.5 billion".
scenes.narration: In Bey v. Indiana, the man who argued that being a Moor made him a sovereign citizen wanted an $11.5 billion refund from the State of Indiana.

scenes.purpose: Show the court's answer to the treaty claim.

visual.description: Bey v. Indiana text; "without any basis in fact" underlines, then "has no immunity from U.S. law" highlights amber.

excerpt.highlight: has no immunity from U.S. law

scenes.narration: The court said the treaty argument is made "without any basis in fact", and that Bey "is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law".

scenes.purpose: Show the common-law version in a promoter's words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "superior" and "inferior" emphasised.
onScreenText: "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government"

scenes.narration: The oldest-sounding version reaches back to the common law, and the National Liberty Alliance teaches that "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government".

scenes.purpose: State what is left of Magna Carta.

visual.description: Title card; "1969" set large; "except for three provisions" smaller beneath.
onScreenText: Magna Carta: repealed by 1969 except for three provisions

citations.label: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.narration: As for Magna Carta, it had been repealed by 1969 except for three provisions.

scenes.purpose: Show an early court dismissing the Magna Carta argument, and Canada's highest court declining to hear it.

visual.description: The review's page; the 1905 High Court quote highlights on s49; on s50 the citation switches to Netolitzky and Warman as the narration turns to Canada.

excerpt.highlight: is not one for serious refutation

citations.label: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand
Netolitzky and Warman, pseudolaw at the Supreme Court of Canada

scenes.narration: As early as 1905, the High Court of Australia said the claim that a law is invalid because it does not conform to Magna Carta "is not one for serious refutation". And the Supreme Court of Canada has refused to hear appeals built on Magna Carta and historical English common law, which the researchers read as a quiet rejection of both.

scenes.purpose: Give the only evidence on paperwork at a stop, and be clear what it does not show.

visual.description: Two stat tiles side by side: "$450" and "$2,000", the low and high prices charged for a "sovereign status" ID card. The note sits small beneath them.

chart.title: Price of a "sovereign status" ID card
chart.note: Sellers' convictions only; the bulletin says nothing about what happened to buyers at a stop.

scenes.direction: Tiles land on their figures; the note fades in on "not what happened to buyers".
scenes.narration: On the papers that are meant to stop police, the evidence is thin: one FBI bulletin reports that three people in Kansas City were convicted for selling "sovereign status" ID cards, at $450 to $2,000 each, that promised immunity from stops and arrests, and it records the sellers' convictions, not what happened to buyers at a stop.

scenes.purpose: Deliver the second answer, then name the narrow parts settled less directly.

visual.description: A large "No" above three labels that build as spoken; on s53 the list dims slightly while the narration names the limits.
onScreenText: Free man under the common law

citations.label: IRS, The Truth About Frivolous Tax Arguments
Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, review of pseudolaw cases in Australia and New Zealand

scenes.direction: Labels build on s52; dim on s53.
scenes.narration: So the answer to the second question is no as well: no court in this evidence has accepted a declared status, whether state national, Moor or free man under the common law. The parts settled less directly are narrow: the federal rulings on state citizenship come from tax cases, so a state court's reach is not what they tested, and the stop question rests on the bulletin above.

scenes.purpose: Tie both answers to one principle.

visual.description: Title card, large; "the law" turns amber.
onScreenText: A court gets its power from the law

scenes.narration: Both answers come down to the same thing: a court gets its power from the law, not from what you write under your name, what hangs on its wall, or what you declare yourself to be.

scenes.purpose: Give the viewer one thing to do.

visual.description: Title card; "one ruling" emphasised.
onScreenText: Ask for one ruling where it worked

scenes.narration: So if someone offers you a form, a code to write by your signature, or a card for the glovebox, ask them for one ruling where it worked.

scenes.purpose: Close by pointing the viewer at the public record.

visual.description: Title card over a soft fade of the court-page backdrop used earlier.

scenes.narration: The rulings where it was tried are public, and they are the place to look before you sign anything.
